title: Surgery + Wounds: Pre-Op, Post-Op, Pressure Injuries

questions.stem: Six days after abdominal surgery, a client coughs, says something gave way, and bowel is coming through the wound. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Gently push the organs back in
Stay with the client, call for help, and cover the organs with sterile saline-moistened dressing
Have the client walk to the bed
Give a meal to settle the stomach

questions.explanation: B is correct: this is evisceration, so stay, call for help, and cover with a sterile saline-moistened dressing. A: never push the organs back in. C is unsafe. D: keep nothing by mouth.

questions.stem: Who explains the procedure and obtains surgical consent?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the provider explains the procedure and gets consent; the nurse witnesses the signature and checks understanding. A only witnesses. C and D don't obtain consent.

questions.stem: Before signing consent, the client seems unsure and is sedated. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the surgery in more detail and witness

questions.explanation: B is correct: if the client is unsure or sedated, stop and call the provider. A and D proceed without valid understanding. C is not taught.

questions.stem: Under current guidelines, until when may healthy clients having planned surgery usually drink clear liquids?
questions.explanation: B is correct: current guidelines allow clear liquids until about two hours before, for healthy clients having planned surgery; fasting follows the anesthesia order. A and C are longer than the limit taught. D is unsafe.

questions.stem: Which actions fit care right after surgery? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check vital signs, the dressing, and bleeding
Expect urine of at least 30 mL an hour
Use the incentive spirometer about 10 times an hour while awake
Keep the client in bed for several days
Check only the breathing rate with opioids

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: airway and breathing first, then circulation, urine at least 30 mL an hour, and the incentive spirometer about 10 times an hour. E: walk early. F: check the sedation level, not just the breathing rate.

questions.stem: After surgery, a client on opioids has a breathing rate of 14 but is very hard to wake. What is the priority?

options.text: Let the client sleep; the rate is normal
Stop the opioid, stimulate, support the airway, and give naloxone per protocol

questions.explanation: B is correct: sedation drops before the breathing rate does, so a normal rate doesn't mean safe; notify the provider too. A and D delay care. C adds more opioid.

questions.stem: A pressure injury shows fat, but no bone. What stage is it?
questions.explanation: C is correct: fat means stage three. A is intact red skin that doesn't blanch. B is shallow with no fat showing. D shows bone, tendon, or muscle.

questions.stem: A client has intact skin over the sacrum with redness that doesn't blanch when pressed. What stage is it?
questions.explanation: A is correct: stage one is intact skin with redness that doesn't blanch. B is a shallow open wound or blister. C is purple or maroon intact skin. D has a base covered by slough or eschar.

questions.stem: A pressure injury's base is covered by a dark scab, so the depth can't be seen. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: C is correct: unstageable means the base is covered by slough or eschar, so you can't see the depth. A and B need a visible base. D is purple or maroon intact skin.

questions.stem: A client's wound edges have separated, but no organs are coming out. What is this called?
questions.explanation: B is correct: dehiscence is wound edges separating without organs coming out; low Fowler's, cover the wound, and notify. A means organs come through. C and D are pressure injuries.
